title: X-rays
sentences: When the editors of De Gids invited me to contribute an essay on the 'X-rays',
whose existence Professor Röntgen at Würzburg demonstrated toward the end of last year, I did not hesitate for a moment to declare myself willing.
That the new phenomena which now occupy the minds of physicists would also awaken keen interest outside their circle
I could take for granted; indeed, in the space of a few months neither any discovery in physics of recent years, nor Hertz's experiments,
nor the detection of argon and helium, has been discussed and written about as much as Röntgen's invisible rays.
Yet I would have objected to saying anything about them in this place,
had the subject not seemed to me pre-eminently suited to a simple treatment intelligible to everyone.
Although the discovery required the resources of a well-equipped laboratory, the apparatus employed
can, at least in essentials, be described very well in brief terms and without the aid of figures.
What mattered was a closed glass tube filled with a highly rarefied gas,
so arranged that powerful electrical discharges could be passed through it; further, around that tube, a sleeve of black cardboard
that cut off every ray of light on its outward path; finally, in the surrounding dark space, a sheet of paper coated with a fluorescent substance, that is,
with a substance that has the property of becoming temporarily luminous itself when irradiated with light.
It did so now too, with every electrical discharge, although
no trace of light was visible; something other than light,
yet something that issued from the discharge apparatus, clearly existed in its vicinity.
The name 'X-rays' chosen by Röntgen refers to rectilinear propagation,
as appears from the 'shadows' that various objects cast upon the fluorescent screen.
It may be mentioned at once that the rays exert a photographic action similar to that of light rays,
that they call forth 'images' on sensitive plates, which can be developed in the ordinary way.
All this can be said in a few words,
and the observations hitherto made could likewise be recounted quickly enough.
I imagine, however, that the reader will also wish to learn something of what happens in the discharge tube.
In these phenomena, which alas still hold almost as many riddles, lies in any case the origin of the X-rays.
By devoting a few pages to them I shall at the same time have occasion
to do justice to some of Röntgen's predecessors.
Of course, this cannot be a comprehensive overview of the discharge symptoms,
starting with the tiny sparks that can be drawn from a rubbed pipe of paint and ending with the tubes that produce the X-rays.
I would like to touch on just a few main points, using some common names and also a certain,
by the way, insofar as it comes into play here, very simple theory of electricity.
There are, as we know, two different and in many respects opposing electrical states.
If one rubs a glass rod against a piece of metal, which is not immediately held in one's hand, but against an 'insulating' stem,
of glass or lacquer, then both are 'electrified' or 'charged', but not in the same way.
A third, also electrified object, if it is attracted by the glass, is repelled by the metal, and vice versa.
The cornerstone of all electricity theory is now the fact that the two states, the 'positive' of the glass,
and the 'negative' of the metal, arise simultaneously; soon this leads to the idea that a certain something of the one
object has passed to the other.
In the image that Benjamin Franklin designed of the phenomena, that 'something' is a substance, the 'electric substance',
or the 'electricity', of which each body in its natural or habitual state contains a certain amount.
Part of this dust would pass from the metal to the glass when rubbed;
the positive charge would exist in an excess above the normal amount, and the negative charge in a deficit.
One can just as well imagine, one is only dealing with an image here,
that the human spirit forms itself from the outside world, that a transition takes place in the opposite direction, from the glass to the metal,
that actually the bodies, which are called positive according to common parlance, have less electricity than in the normal state.
Finally, it is also possible, and I will make use of this view here, to use two substances with opposite properties,
the positive and the negative electricity; in the natural state, each body with the same amount of
one as provided with the other substance, but the friction brings about a change in this distribution;
it delivers more positive than negative electricity to the glass, but more negative than positive electricity to the metal.
There are already a few electricity theories that can each be further elaborated in many different ways.
However, all these views have one trait in common, a trait that is most sharply expressed,
if one briefly and plainly labels electricity—or the two electricities—with the name 'substance', this namely:
that electricity is never produced, but that it is only moved and that the electrical balance is thereby broken.
This is done at any time and for the most diverse reasons, when ironing with a feather over a sheet of paper,
a piece of iron is lying on the damp ground,
a magnet is moved in the vicinity of a copper wire, a quartz crystal is compressed or the contact point of two bodies is heated.
Here in the small; in the big,
when the power of a waterfall sets a tool in motion, generating a mighty electric current.
On a lofty scale in nature, as the clouds of the storm gather.
That man can understand the electrical phenomena scientifically
can investigate and serve the fulfillment of his needs, is largely due to the tools,
allowing the electricity to be moved, as well as water to be set in motion by a pump.
'electricity pumps' now come in many forms; all electrification machines, galvanic elements, alternators, induction bobbins can be called such.
They all have two poles , two pieces of metal usually, one of which acquires a positive and the other a negative charge;
the significance of the tool lies precisely in the fact that it drives positive electricity from one pole to the other.
The poles themselves can therefore be compared with nothing better than with two bins,
so connected to a pump that water is sucked out of one tank and squeezed into the other.
It is now only possible to imagine that
the bins are separated from each other only by a thin partition wall and that these are under the pressure of the
one side of the accumulated water collapses,
to obtain an image of the electrical spark between two metal spheres that are connected by guide wires to the poles of an electrifying machine.
As long as the urge of positive electricity to one and negative electricity to the other bulb is not too great,
the air between the conductors can resist the tendency of electricity to pass from one body to another,
but finally under heat and light development and with crackling sound
the positive charge of one sphere and the negative charge of the other sphere are equalised.
Two important questions arise right now.
The space between the spheres does not contain a single substance, but two substances, first of all the air,
and secondly, the ether, whose light phenomena have revealed their existence.
The air, consisting of countless separated particles, molecules,
of which one knows that they fly back and forth at speeds of a few hundred meters per second, incessantly colliding with each other.
The ether, which may also have a molecular structure, but may just as well be a 'continuum'.
Which is it, the air or the ether, which first opens the passage to the electric
time, and what substance is most involved when the discharge finally takes place?
To resolve this, it was necessary to remove the air,
or at least dilute it, and see what becomes of the discharge.
In this way, the answer to the questions just asked has been found and, in addition, numerous other surprising and curious results have been obtained.
The knowledge one has of the electrical discharge phenomena is therefore largely responsible for
the improvement of the air pumps.
For a long time, one had no other than the well-known piston air pump,
with which the air in a vessel can be diluted to something like one 500th of the original amount.
Much further, one can bring it with the mercury air pump, which was first constructed by Geissler in Bonn in 1857, and which,
especially through later improvements, has become an admirable tool, an indispensable tool in the laboratory and in the factories of electric light bulbs.
In principle, the setup is very simple.
A glass sphere is fused to the upper end of a vertical tube, also made of - glass,
through which one can in one way or another cause a quantity of mercury to rise and fall in turn.
The sphere can be placed in communion with the space from which it is desired to remove the air;
in addition, a path to the outside air can be opened at the top end.
In the original Geissler tool, a single glass crane with suitable holes serves one as well as the other.
While the road to the outside air is open, the mercury is allowed to completely fill the sphere;
after all the air has thus been driven out of the sphere, this road is closed off, and now, as the mercury drops,
community between the pump and the empty vessel, so that the air from the latter spreads over the space above the falling mercury.
These operations are repeated a large number of times.
It soon became apparent that there were difficulties with the piston air pump,
because there are much greater defects, had not noticed them, but they have been able to overcome them in an excellent way.
In order to free the airless space from all water vapour, a ball was connected to the mercury air pump with anhydrous phosphoric acid,
an independence that eagerly takes in the water vapour.
But also other
substances than water were found to emit vapours, in particular the fat that,
in however small quantities, until sealing of the tap and of various connection points was necessary.
They have therefore omitted all taps and invented other tools,
through which one can force the air to go exactly where one wants it.
Furthermore, if the glass vessel that one wants to pump out is melted to a glass tube,
which, on the other hand, is connected to the air pump in the same way, one has a completely airtight closure,
and the 'vacuum' is in contact with nothing but glass, mercury and phosphoric acid.
Add to this the fact that the layer of air adhering to the glass walls can be loosened by heating them during evacuation,
that electrical discharges can also promote this, and finally that, in order to achieve good results, one must take comfort,
to continue the operation for hours or even days, one has obtained a sufficient idea of working with a mercury air pump.
At the dilution, which can finally be achieved under favorable conditions,
perhaps only the millionth part of the original amount of air is still present in the barrel.
Is the vessel connected to the mercury air pump intended for electrical discharge testing,
then a few metal wires are attached to it beforehand, the 'electrodes', which will be connected to the poles of the electromagnet or of the inductor.
Platinum wires can be inserted halfway in through a small opening in the glass wall and then fused; i.e.,
by heating, the glass can be allowed to flow together along the circumference of the wire in such a way that the opening is completely closed.
The 'vacuum tube' can remain connected to the mercury air pump during the discharge tests, or be separated from it first.
This is done by heating the connecting tube with a small flame in a place that has previously been constricted by extraction.
The outside air squeezes the softened glass wall and a small movement is sufficient to bring about the desired separation.
In this way, the well-known Geissler tubes were manufactured,
which come in a wide variety of shapes and sizes, and many of which are true works of art of glassblowing.
The first thing that catches the eye with these tubes is the ease with which they allow the electrical discharge to pass through.
If one gives electricity the choice between a path through the ordinary air, over two spheres, which e.g.
at a distance of half an inch from each other, and the way through a Geissler tube,
where the electrodes are a few decimeters apart, she prefers the last way.
The air thus turns out to be an impediment and one tends to expect that with continued dilution the transition of electricity will take place more and more easily,
that a space without any air, only filled with the ether,
- which we have no control over, since it passes through the glass, - would be an excellent conductor of electricity.
Unfortunately, that’s often not the case.
The ordinary Geissler tubes are namely
not pumped at all as far as can be done with all the precautions described above.
At higher degrees of dilution, the passage of electricity becomes more difficult again,
and finally a spark of a few centimetres in air from
the normal density, then a discharge occurs in a vacuum tube in which the electrodes are somewhat less distant from each other.
Tubes have even been made, which refuse to allow the discharge of very powerful induction coils to pass through.
In view of these phenomena, it is safe to assume that the discharge always takes place with the cooperation of the gas.
Should it be objected that the amount of air in the pipes is so small,
then it should be remembered that 'small' is only a relative concept.
Estimates are made of the number of air molecules present in a cubic millimeter, an estimate determined by the study of
the properties of the gases has become possible, the best vacuum tubes will be worth thousands of millions.
I will come back to the role that gas plays later.
For the moment, the light phenomena that accompany the discharge are of more importance,
and which have undergone very drastic changes in the dilution of the air.
The width of the luminous gas has also increased at the same time as the length of the path between the electrodes;
indeed, the light can completely fill the cross-section of tubes of a few centimetres in diameter.
If one now considers a luminous Geissler tube, one is struck by a very remarkable under-
separation between the environment of the positive pole or 'anode' and that of the negative pole or 'cathode'.
By the way, such a difference can also be very well noticed at the ordinary density of the air.
With the Holtz electrifier and many others, there are two pairs of metal spikes, which are turned towards a rotating glass disc.
If the machine is in operation, positive electricity passes from one set to the disc and negative electricity from the other,
and in the dark you can see a light development in both.
However, while the positive light has the form of long violet plumes, the negative spires only exist as small dots of light.
This negative 'glow' deserves all the more to be mentioned here, because, as it will turn out, the germ of the X-rays lies in it.
In an ordinary Geissler tube, one has both positive and negative light;
however, these phenomena cover very uneven parts of the internal space.
However, the glow is much more expansive than at the tips of the electrification machine,
but it is still determined to a luminous layer of a few millimetres or perhaps a centimetre thick, which covers the cathode.
The positive light, on the other hand, extends from the anode through almost the entire length of the tube,
even though it is many decimeters and even though the tube is bent into whimsical shapes and sometimes narrowed, then widened again;
it first ends close to the cathode, where it is separated from the glow light by a dark space.
It is therefore the positive light that has attracted the most attention for a long time.
Due to its colourful splendour, which varies with the nature of the gas, and its enigmatic alternating light and dark layers, it offers an attractive spectacle,
whose beauty can be further enhanced by locally constricting or widening the tube and surrounding it with fluorescent liquids,
or a tube that is made entirely or partially of a fluorescent type of glass.
The weighty trials of Hittorf in Münster opened a new era in the study of discharge in 1868.
He first worked with much higher dilutions than in
the ordinary Geissler tubes and now saw how the glow was already further and further away from the
cathode, while the positive light fades into the background.
It is true, however, that as dilution continues, the cathode light becomes weaker and weaker,
but even though it is hardly visible anymore, it always retains its property, wherever it comes into contact with the glass wall,
these with a green colour can be made to fluoresce brightly;
from the placement and the size of the light spot on the glass, a decision can therefore be made about the extent of the glowlight.
Highly remarkable now is the fact discovered by Hittorf that at high dilutions
the development of the negative light becomes independent of the location of the anode.
One can draw from a straight line in the thought of any point of the cathode,
that is perpendicular to its surface; these lines will all be within a certain space,
which is delimited on one side by the cathode and on the other side by the glass wall.
Well, it's closest to this space, which is occupied by the glow.
Is e.g.
used as the cathode a disc of aluminium, which is attached in a perpendicular position to the end of a fused wire,
then a cylinder of glow light develops at the front of the disc, which,
when the cathode is attached to one end of a long tube, can extend over the full length.
It could be, viz.
when the anode is placed at the other end of the tube, that the glow cylinder now actually reaches the anode,
but even then it does not have to be completely absorbed by it, but can partially hit the glass wall.
When Hittorf used a lateral wire as anode,
placed in the middle of the length of the tube and bent so that it ran along the axis of the tube for some distance,
this wire was washed by the glow cylinder, without seeming to have any influence on it.
Another time, a wire placed and bent over in the manner mentioned above was used as the cathode.
With the exception of the end surface, it was enclosed in a glass tube, so that the glow could only develop on that surface.
From there it extended to the end of the tube,
where the bent wire was turned, and that even when the anode was at the other end; a proof
that the glow, in its extension away from the negative electrode, can even move away from the anode.
With a tube like the latter, it is now also very eye-catching,
what an important difference there is between the positive and the negative light.
The first does look for the negative electrode, as it turns out, when the two poles are exchanged with each other.
The positive light can, as far as one knows,
in a bent or kinked tube as far as in a straight tube of otherwise the same nature.
The negative light, on the other hand, limited as it is to the above-mentioned space, can never turn a corner.
This is clearly seen in a tube that has the shape of a V, with the electrodes at the highest points.
The glow remains in one leg and cannot do anything else at the bottom other than the glass,
that it comes into contact with, to fluoresce.
All these phenomena give rise to the suspicion that the glow light propagates away from the cathode in straight lines,
and have given rise to the name 'cathode rays,' a term that,
to make one more argument, everyone will be able to unite, who has observed how different objects, metal plates e.g.,
placed in the tube on the path of the glowlight, cast a dark shadow on the fluorescent glass wall.
Incidentally, the name 'cathode rays' is slightly above that of 'glowing light.'
It has already been mentioned that at high dilutions the latter becomes fainter and fainter.
One therefore does one's best to imagine that,
in the undisturbed development of cathode rays, there is absolutely no 'light' emanating from the space they occupy.
This arises first, as an additional phenomenon, when the rays are intercepted,
either through the glass wall, or through the air itself, which is still in the tube.
By the way, everything that captivates the eye in the positive light of Geissler's tubes,
is only a result of the movement of electricity, which is invisible to us.
At the meeting of the British Association in 1879, Crookes,
to whom one already owed the well-known radiometer, see a series of clean tests on cathode rays.
By the title of his lecture: 'on radiant matter' he gave
expression of a certain hypothesis about the nature of rays.
According to Crookes, tiny particles with a negative electrical charge, either those that already had,
or first obtained at the surface of the cathode, repelled by the latter at great speed; they fly in straight lines,
and the bombardment of these small projectiles against the glass wall generates vibrations,
that create the impression of light in the eye of the observer; this is the fluorescence of the glass.
This view finds a powerful support in the mechanical action of the cathode rays on objects, as a result of which they are captured.
In one of its vacuum spheres, Crookes had enclosed a light mill, a cross made of aluminium,
that rested on a marker with a glass cap, in the manner of a compass needle.
The horizontal arms carried small vertically placed mica plates at the end as wicks; these became, as the cross rotated,
each in turn laterally affected by the cathode rays, which emanated from an electrode placed in a side tube.
As soon as the inductor was put into operation, the mill went into rapid rotation.
Also a 'reaction wheel', similar to the known devices that are made to run by the outflow of water or steam,
or with the 'rotating suns' of the fireworks makers, was constructed by Crookes.
The blades of the mill were now made of aluminum, so that they could serve as cathodes themselves,
when the metal needle carrying the cross, this time with a metal cap, was connected to the one pole of the induction reel.
Since each wick was lined on one side with an insulating fabric,
cathode rays could only arise on the other side; whereas here, always according to Crookes' view,
the small projectiles were pushed away, the wick itself had to experience a force in the opposite direction.
That this force really existed was demonstrated by the rapid rotation of the mill.
Crookes' theory has not gone unchallenged.
For the moment, I will let her rest here, to stay with the further experimental research.
An important step was taken in 1893 by Lenard in Bonn.
The cathode rays would of course become much more accessible,
if they could be taken outside the vacuum tube, and the way was open for this,
after Hertz had observed that very thin gold or aluminum leaf, placed in the path of the rays, allows them to pass through.
Lenard now provided his tube with a window of aluminum, and indeed, the rays came out through it in the air.
One will feel lightly that the test was not easy.
The window must be very thin, it will let the cathode rays through; it must be very small,
in order to be able to resist the pressure of the outside air at the low thickness.
Lenard closed his tube at one end with a metal plate, in which was a round opening of 1.7 m.M. diameter;
the aluminium sheet glued to the edge thereof was only 1/400 m.M. thick.
The goal was now really achieved, although the rays did not penetrate far into the air.
Up to a distance of three centimeters, if the light of the discharge tube was carefully shut off,
a faint blue light twilight visible in the sky,
which Lenard compares with what one sees when one lets light fall through a slit in a cloudy liquid, e.g.
in milk.
The air is apparently cloudy against the cathode rays, and as it blocks and scatters them, it itself becomes luminous,
as was already noticed above from the air in the tube.
Better still than through the observation of the light of the sky, an idea could be obtained of the expansion of the rays,
by placing a screen in the vicinity of the window, which was covered with an easily fluorescent substance.
The light from this drowned out that of the air and could still be seen from a distance of 8 centimetres.
Another tool was the photographic effect of the rays.
Lenard has extensively investigated the translucency of all kinds of fabrics.
Strangely, there is a big difference in this respect between the cathode rays and the light.
A quartz plate ½ millimeter thick cast a dark shadow,
while from a thin aluminium leaf, opaque to light, the shadow was barely detectable.
To Lenard's treatise has been added the reproduction of a photograph, which shows this; it has been taken,
while the sensitive plate was locked in a small space, entirely bounded by metal walls; the wall, by the way, facing the
window, consisted of aluminium with a thickness of 1/250 millimetres.
While the degree of transparency to the rays of light depends greatly on the nature of the bodies,
lenard has shown that the cathode rays only or almost only ask about the amount of dust,
by the mass or weight of it, which they meet on their way.
If one body is replaced by another, the density of which is twice as high,
then the thickness of the layer must be halved to obtain the same translucency.
It also turned out that the window could be made of thin glass, instead of aluminium.
Of all previous researchers, Lenard has come closest to discovering the X-rays.
However, it was up to Röntgen to connect his name to rays emanating from the glass wall of the vacuum tube,
without a window, and even if the thickness is perhaps a millimeter,
and that far surpasses Lenard's rays in the ability to penetrate air and other bodies.
How the tests were taken has already been mentioned.
Undoubtedly, workings in
the area around the tube and certainly a very trained eye was needed to find the first trace.
Röntgen first used a screen with barium platinum cyanide, which fluoresced even up to a distance of 2 meters,
and then came to the photography with the X-rays, so that the phenomena can be studied much more calmly and the advantage is obtained that
one can still perceive weak rays by extending the duration of the pose, even if it is up to an hour or more.
Since the photographs are treated in the usual way, the places,
where the sensitive plate is most affected by the rays, later in the 'positive' the lightest.
As far as translucency is concerned, Röntgen found the following.
Paper shines through so much that clear fluorescence could be seen behind a bound book of 1000 pages or behind a double whist game.
Wood and ebonite are still translucent at a thickness of several centimetres.
Water, carbon disulfide and various other liquids were examined after being placed in micro-walled trays
cast, and turned out to be very translucent.
Particularly surprising is the ability of the jets to penetrate rather thick metal plates;
aluminium allows the X-rays as well as the cathode rays to pass through more than any other metal and could even be several millimetres thick.
The least translucent are platinum and lead; the first metal about 200, the last about 70 times less than aluminum.
At a thickness of 1.5 millimetres, lead allowed virtually nothing to pass through and communicates the property to lead-containing glass and lead paint,
pretty much absorb a lot of the rays.
One sees nothing when one catches the rays in the eye,
even if this is kept close to the discharge tube, and no light phenomenon is detected on the path of the rays through the air,
as is the case with the cathode rays, which are therefore more strongly absorbed.
Reproduction takes place along straight lines and
the rays do not even deviate from this when they pass from one substance into another.
While all kinds of light and also various other 'invisible' rays known for a long time,
as the dark heat rays change direction at the passage through a prism, nothing has been detected at the X-rays,
although it has been tested with prisms of water, carbon disulphide, ebonite and aluminium.
A regular reflection, as the light undergoes through a mirror, has also not been observed;
but with some metal plates a so-called diffuse reflection, something similar to when light falls on a sheet of paper.
Photographing with the rays of Röntgen differs in two respects from photographing with light.
First of all, even if one does not want to, as in the first tests, enclose the discharge tube itself in a slightly impermeable casing,
wrap the sensitive plate in black paper or leave it in a closed châssis, as the X-rays penetrate paper and wood.
One can then work in full daylight and even,
as has been done repeatedly, photographing through a plate of ebonite or an aluminium sheet.
Secondly, no lenses can be used,
since the rays are not refracted by the glass and therefore cannot be concentrated into 'images'.
All the photographs made show shadow images, and are undoubtedly made for the most part, while the object
was kept at a small distance from the sensitive plate.
At a somewhat large distance, due to the extent of the radiation source, the shadows do not become sharp,
unless this problem is remedied by using only the jets that pass through an opening that is not too large.
The important applications that these photographs have already found are based on the fact that one can see the shadows of opaque objects,
even if they are enclosed by substances that do not allow light to pass through;
it is sufficient that these substances are more or less translucent to the X-rays.
Among the most surprising photographs soon obtained by the discoverer are those of a compass needle,
enclosed in a metal sheath, on which the partial stripes of the rose can also be seen very clearly,
of a metal wire, hidden from the eye between two wooden discs, and above all of a hand,
on which the dark shadows of the bones are clearly visible amid the lighter shadows of the soft parts.
Besides, these images have already become so widely known that nothing more needs to be said about them.
Nor is it necessary to mention the countless repetitions of the tests on a large and small scale.
I am permitted to say only about the nature of the phenomenon,
although it cannot be done otherwise than to mention a few assumptions, between which presumably the further investigation will have to decide.
First of all, it is certain that the X-rays are something different from Lenard's rays.
Already their greater penetration points to this and there is, as will soon become apparent, a second difference.
With all that, the rays of Röntgen, as well as those of Lenard,
in one way or another from the cathode rays in the tube;
it has been found that they always start from that part of the glass wall that is affected by the cathode rays and caused to fluoresce.
Therefore, before one enters into reflections on the nature of the X-rays,
again to return to the cathode rays in the tube.
Was Crookes right when he declared it to be radiant matter?
Many physicists doubt this and prefer to see vibrations in the cathode rays, which propagate from the cathode into the ether,
something similar to a beam of light, although of course the vibrations must be of a different nature than those of light.
The proponents of this opinion invoke, as far as Crookes' spinning mills are concerned,
on the fact that, according to light theory, a beam of light exerts a pressure on every object that causes it to become a parent, and therefore,
which is closely related to this, a body that emits light rays on one side itself experiences a force in the opposite direction.
Such a, perhaps stronger effect could also have the vibrations of the cathode rays, if there are vibrations.
Lenard carried out further tests, in which the discharge tube was separated by the aluminium window from a room that was also connected to a mercury air pump.
Now while that space was being evacuated, he saw the cathode rays penetrating further and further into it,
finally, to a distance of more than a meter, and this phenomenon persisted,
even though such a completely empty space had been reached that no electrical discharges could take place in the said space itself.
The cathode rays can therefore reproduce in a space in which they can no longer arise ,
most likely also in the ether, when it is freed of all air molecules.
Therefore, Lenard believes, they must be phenomena in the ether;
they must consist in a vibration or a disturbance of equilibrium of this or that nature, which reproduces in the ether.
It is not the place here to carefully weigh the different opinions against each other.
Still, I cannot restrain the statement that Crookes' view seems to me to be the most plausible.
Against Lenard's remark mentioned above, it can be argued that small projectiles,
that have penetrated through the aluminum window, will be able to move very well in a space that contains only ether.
However, the fact that one really has to deal with such projectiles is argued by two facts.
The first is the small speed of the cathode rays compared to the light.
J.P.J.
Thomson at Cambridge has
proved by ingenious tests that two points of the tube wall,
of which one was 10 centimetres further away from the cathode than the other, did not begin to fluoresce at the same time.
The place furthest from the cathode did this a little later than the other;
the time difference was about a two-millionth of a second.
While these tests justify the opinion that the cathode is really the point of exit of the rays,
they also prove that a road of 200,000 meters is travelled per second.
This speed is now, for vibrations, very small.
The light passes through a distance of 300,000,000 meters in one second, and in what we know of the ether,
is nothing that indicates the possibility of vibrations at a slower rate of propagation.
The second fact referred to above is the peculiar influence of magnetic forces on the course of the cathode rays.
Rectilinear propagation ceases as soon as a magnetic pole is brought into the vicinity of a Crookes tube.
The curved line that the beams then follow corresponds perfectly to the path,
in which, under the same conditions, negatively charged particles emanating from the cathode would move.
For vibration theory, on the other hand, the operation of a magnet has so far been an unsolved mystery.
Lenard's rays are as sensitive to magnetic influences as the cathode rays in the tube;
they are therefore most likely of the same nature and must, in the theory that seems most likely to me,
are also considered to be a stream of negatively charged particles, either that the particles in the tube have flown through the window, or,
what is less simple is that their bumps against the aluminium drive other particles out of the metal.
Those who want to assume the first should also imagine that the projectiles are smaller than air molecules in their entirety,
since the window for the latter is impenetrable.
By the way, there are many reasons to believe that the molecules of all bodies contain much smaller particles, so-called 'ions',
equipped with electric charges; these ions, and not the molecules themselves, could be at play with the cathode rays.
The development of the rays in the tube is also consistent with this view

On average, a molecule can only fly in air of normal density over a distance of 1/10,000 millimetres without colliding with another particle;
it follows that, after dilution to 1/10000 of the original density, the free path will be about 1 millimeter.
Since cathode rays of much greater length can now develop at this dilution, one must imagine smaller projectiles,
that can penetrate further between the molecules and perhaps even through a molecule, between the atoms of which it is composed.
Considerations such as the communicated, how appropriate perhaps to ignite some light about the nature of
the cathode rays and the rays of Lenard leave the question of the nature of the X-rays undecided.
The propagation speed is not yet known and there is no function of a magnet here;
strong magnetic forces even do not direct the X-rays away from the right path.
Therefore, the arguments that argue in favour of Crookes' theory with regard to the cathode rays are dropped here.
However, it remains conceivable that small particles fly through the glass, or are pushed away from it,
- in which case the insensitivity to magnetic influences should be explained by the lack of an electrical charge or by a very high speed -,
but the phenomena do not forbid it either,
to see in the X-ray beams the propagation of a wave movement of a special kind, as is suspected from different sides.
The hypotheses that have already been proposed have this use, that they can point the way to decisive experiments.
That these will not be long in coming and that perhaps after a few months the riddle will mainly be solved,
may be expected with a view to the tools of contemporary physics.
It would be unfair to end this essay without saying a single word about Goldstein's investigations in Berlin.
More than anyone else, he has studied the light phenomena in the discharge tubes in detail.
Even before Lenard, he showed that the cathode rays are photographically active and in 1886 he proved
that in a vacuum tube, in addition to the cathode rays, rays can be generated on which a magnet does not work.
The details of this discovery, as well as what Goldstein found further, had to be omitted here;
his results will prove to be of great value, however, when the time has come that we now see approaching,
on which the discharge phenomena and the X-rays will grant us a new look into the essence of the molecules and the aether.
